title: ShapeRNA: an integrated web server for RNA secondary structure, ensemble, and functional analysis

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unpacked the Europe PMC supplement (1.12 MB zip): it holds only 7 figure images and one 1.04 MB PDF of supplementary notes/figures, no data tables; I extracted the PDF's text and its only tables are prose comparisons of tools and platforms, with no rows of measurements. I fetched https://shaperna.com twice: it returns the 'InCommon Federation Discovery Service' page, i.e. a redirect to a University of Florida Shibboleth single sign-on login, so the advertised server was not usable without an institutional account when I checked. The one linked data source, a Code Ocean capsule of HIV-1 RRE sequencing reads, returned HTTP 403 (forbidden) both on the page and the application programming interface endpoint. I searched the full open-access text (61 kB) for any download, dataset, benchmark or training-set link and found none.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the server runs on an AMD EPYC machine with 64 GB RAM, that the three case studies used MAPT exon 10, a 91-nucleotide HIV-1 Rev Response Element region and the HULC long non-coding RNA, and that the Code Ocean capsule contains FASTQ sequencing files. I did not see any of those files.

a1_downloadable.note: There is no dataset to download. The paper distributes a web tool, not data; https://shaperna.com redirected me to a University of Florida single sign-on login page (contradicting the paper's 'no login requirement'), and the only linked data, a Code Ocean capsule of HIV-1 sequencing reads, returned HTTP 403 (forbidden). The supplement contains figures and notes only.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: No label column exists anywhere. To get any prediction target you would have to run the server (or its underlying tools) on sequences you supply, i.e. construct both the features and the label from scratch.

a3_inputs_present.note: The only inputs named are two GenBank accessions (HG975403.1 for HULC, Gene ID 4137 for MAPT) and one 91-nucleotide HIV-1 region; three sequences, all referenced rather than tabulated.

a4_units_stated.note: Not applicable in a harmful way: the quantities mentioned (free energy in kcal/mol, chemical probing reactivity) carry conventional units, but there is no table of them to check.

a5_enough_rows.note: Three case-study RNAs (MAPT exon 10, a 91-nucleotide HIV-1 Rev Response Element, HULC). Far under the ~1,500-row bar; counted from the paper's own case-study list, since no file exists.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small, because there is essentially nothing there.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be assessed: there are no counts in any file to compare against the paper.

a8_label_provenance.note: Every structure shown in the paper is the output of another prediction program (RNAfold, RNAstructure, UFold, MXfold2, Seismic and others wrapped by the server). Training on these would be distilling those tools, which is exactly the circularity A8 forbids.

existing_models.name: UFold (deep learning RNA secondary structure predictor, Nucleic Acids Research 2022)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported F1 (harmonic mean of precision and recall) of 0.91 on ArchiveII, a standard 3,975-structure benchmark, versus 0.77 for MXfold2; figures taken from search-result summaries of the UFold paper, not from re-running it.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalisation to RNA families not seen during training; later reviews single this out as the open problem.

existing_models.name: MXfold2 (thermodynamics-constrained deep learning folder)
existing_models.score_and_split: F1 of 0.77 on ArchiveII per the same comparison; its thermodynamic constraint is credited with better out-of-family behaviour.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Accuracy on families absent from training data.

existing_models.name: BPfold (base-pair motif energy model, Nature Communications 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Claims superior accuracy and generalisation to unseen families against prior state of the art; I saw the abstract-level claim in search results only, no numbers verified.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Out-of-distribution RNA families remain the stated bottleneck.

existing_models.name: DEPfold (ICLR 2025, dependency-parsing formulation)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported F1 of 0.920 on ArchiveII, the highest in the comparison I retrieved; number from a search-result summary.

existing_models.name: ShapeRNA itself (this paper)
existing_models.score_and_split: No benchmark, no accuracy number and no evaluation is reported anywhere in the paper; it is a wrapper that runs other people's tools.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The authors frame fragmentation across tools, not accuracy, as the problem they solve.

backbone.name: RNA-FM (RNA language model) or the Ribonanza-trained chemical-probing models
backbone.hardware: Would be viable on a 16 GB laptop for short RNAs, but there is no labelled data here to attach a head to.

integration.partner_dataset: None usable. In principle bpRNA/ArchiveII (curated RNA structures) or the Ribonanza chemical-probing set could be joined, but neither is this paper's data.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: No combined question can be written, because this paper contributes no measurements to combine.

controls.positive_control: None available: with three RNAs there is nothing to hold out.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim can be made from this paper's data, because it contains three example RNA sequences and no measured outcomes.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use RNA sequence to predict which bases pair with which, and how reactive each base is to chemical probing.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would train on RNA sequences with experimentally determined base pairings. This paper supplies three such sequences, so the training data would have to come entirely from elsewhere (ArchiveII, bpRNA, Ribonanza).
plain_idea.predict: Base-pairing partners per nucleotide, or per-nucleotide chemical reactivity. The true answer comes from comparative sequence analysis, crystal/cryo-EM structures, or SHAPE/DMS chemical probing experiments — none of which this paper performed.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: RNA structure prediction matters for splicing, viral biology and RNA drug design, but this particular paper offers no new measurements, so nothing here would advance it.

more_or_better_data.why: This paper supplies three example RNAs. UFold, MXfold2 and BPfold were trained on thousands of curated structures (ArchiveII alone has 3,975), and the Ribonanza competition released chemical probing for hundreds of thousands of sequences.

confidence_score.why: There are no replicate measurements and no per-item uncertainty in anything this paper distributes, so no calibrated confidence could be estimated from it.

models_beatable.why: The best reported numbers I found are from 2025 (BPfold in Nature Communications, DEPfold at ICLR with F1 0.920 on ArchiveII) and the field has already moved to explicitly out-of-family evaluation, so the easy wins on weak splits are gone.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition outright: there is no dataset from this paper for our model to see in addition to what the baseline sees.

ml_idea: None viable from this paper. The only conceivable project — benchmarking the folding tools ShapeRNA wraps against each other on out-of-family RNAs — would use ArchiveII/bpRNA/Ribonanza data that has nothing to do with this paper, and several 2025 papers have already done exactly that.

effort.compute_note: No compute estimate is meaningful: the only files are a 1.12 MB supplement of figures and a PDF of notes. Nothing was timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open the supplement and the data availability statement and count the data tables. There are zero, and the three named sequences are the whole dataset — ten minutes of work kills this.

verdict_reason: ShapeRNA is a web server that wraps a dozen existing RNA folding programs; it publishes no dataset at all. Part A fails on A1 (nothing downloadable — the server URL redirected me to a University of Florida single sign-on login and the linked Code Ocean capsule returned HTTP 403), A2 and A3 (no label column, no feature table, three referenced sequences), A5 (n=3 RNAs), and A8 (every structure in the paper is another model's output, so training on it would be distillation, not biology). The underlying task is also one of the most crowded in computational RNA biology, with open models from 2022-2025 already evaluated on out-of-family splits.
